narrative:
The model estimated a 67% chance that you will fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because your law school application was tied to this prediction, that high failure risk led to rejection.

The strongest reason was your third-year class standing: you were in the lowest decile, compared with an average of about the sixth decile among accepted students. This pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. Your first-year class standing was also in the lowest decile, versus an average of about the sixth decile, and it was the third most influential factor, again increasing failure risk. The second most influential factor was your LSAT score of 36, slightly below the accepted-student average of about 37. Even so, in this prediction that score acted as a counterweight toward passing rather than as the main cause of denial. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.50 is also below the accepted average, though it was not among the top three drivers.

Next, ask admissions for feedback, and focus on the areas the prediction weighted most: build a stronger academic record or explain your early class standing, consider retaking the LSAT if practice results suggest a meaningful gain, and seek pre-law advising about delaying or strengthening your application with relevant legal work or coursework.
